clinicalPearls: NMO is an aggressive antibody-mediated inflammatory CNS disorder defined by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis; the broader term NMOSD captures partial forms and cases with additional CNS involvement (Harrison p.3590).
Strongly female-predominant (women:men roughly 9:1), with a mean onset around age 40 but possible at any age (Harrison p.3590).

Optic neuritis in NMO can be bilateral and cause severe vision loss, a pattern uncommon in MS; myelitis is often severe, transverse, and longitudinally extensive spanning three or more contiguous vertebral segments (Harrison p.3590).
Unlike MS, NMO rarely follows a progressive course; accumulated disability results from attack-related injury rather than progression (Harrison p.3590).

Brain MRI is not invariably normal: lesions may involve the area postrema (intractable hiccups or vomiting), hypothalamus (sleep disorder or endocrinopathy), or cerebral hemispheres; large hemispheric lesions can be asymptomatic, show a 'cloud-like' appearance, be non-destructive, and resolve completely (Harrison p.3590).
Spinal cord lesions are focal enhancing areas of swelling and tissue destruction over three or more segments and are centered on the gray matter on axial imaging (Harrison p.3590).

CSF typically shows greater pleocytosis than MS, sometimes with neutrophils and eosinophils in acute cases, while oligoclonal bands are uncommon (present in fewer than 20% of patients) (Harrison p.3590-3591).

A highly specific serum autoantibody against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) is present in about 90% of patients and is diagnostic when paired with a typical clinical presentation (Harrison p.3590).
In a subset of AQP4-negative cases, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) are found (Harrison p.3591).

Up to 40% of NMO patients have a coexisting systemic autoimmune disorder (e.g., SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, p-ANCA vasculitis, myasthenia gravis, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mixed connective tissue disease) - a feature distinguishing it from MS (Harrison p.3591).
Symptomatic onset may follow acute infection with varicella-zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, or tuberculosis; rare cases are paraneoplastic (breast, lung, or other cancers) (Harrison p.3592).
Asian and African ancestry populations are disproportionately affected, with the highest reported prevalence in Martinique; among white populations MS is far more common than NMO (Harrison p.3591).
harrison.pathophysiology: NMO is an autoimmune astrocytopathy driven by autoantibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4), which is concentrated on astrocyte foot processes apposed to endothelium and at paranodal regions near nodes of Ranvier. Pathology shows loss of AQP4 staining with antibody and complement deposition, astrocyte cytolysis, thickened vessel walls, demyelination, and inflammation. AQP4 antibodies are likely pathogenic, since passive transfer reproduces disease features in animals; both complement fixation and antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity contribute to astrocyte injury, and TH17 proinflammatory T cells recognizing an immunodominant AQP4 epitope may also participate. A thymic B-cell population that constitutively expresses AQP4 normally interacts with AQP4-specific T cells to maintain tolerance, and impairment of this interaction may contribute. During acute myelitis attacks, CSF levels of IL-6 and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) are markedly elevated, reflecting active inflammation and astrocyte injury (Harrison p.3590-3591).
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis (especially opticospinal MS subtype in Asian/African ancestry, which can itself be AQP4-seropositive and represent NMOSD)
Systemic autoimmune myelopathy (SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, Behcet's disease)
Spinal cord infarction (longitudinally extensive anterior cord syndrome)
infectionMimics: Viral myelitis (e.g., herpes simplex virus type 2 causing recurrent myelitis)
additionalInvestigations: Serum AQP4-IgG testing using a cell-based assay (strongly recommended detection method)
Spinal cord MRI to demonstrate longitudinally extensive (>=3 segment) gray matter-centered lesions
Brain MRI to detect area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, or cloud-like hemispheric lesions
Optic nerve MRI (T2/gadolinium-enhancing lesion over >half optic nerve length or chiasm)
Lumbar puncture for CSF pleocytosis, cell differential, and oligoclonal bands
Screening for coexisting systemic autoimmune disease
redFlags: Bilateral simultaneous optic neuritis with severe vision loss
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments
Intractable hiccups, nausea, or vomiting (area postrema syndrome)
Acute brainstem or diencephalic syndrome (e.g., symptomatic narcolepsy, hypothalamic dysfunction)
Recurrent attacks, since more than half of untreated AQP4-seropositive patients relapse within 1 year
harrison.prognosis: NMO is typically a relapsing disease; a monophasic course occurs in fewer than 10% of patients and is somewhat more likely in AQP4-antibody-negative individuals. Untreated disease is severely disabling: historically about one-third of patients developed respiratory failure from cervical myelitis, and by 8 years roughly 60% were blind and more than half had permanent limb paralysis. AQP4-seropositive patients carry a high relapse risk (more than half relapse within 1 year if untreated). Long-term outcomes have substantially improved with the advent of attack and relapse therapies, with reported 5-year survival rising from about 68-75% around 1999 to 91-98% by 2017 (Harrison p.3590-3591).
pitfalls: Assuming a normal brain MRI excludes NMO - characteristic area postrema, periependymal brainstem, diencephalic, and cloud-like hemispheric lesions can be present (Harrison p.3590).
Conflating NMO with MS: bilateral severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, marked CSF pleocytosis, and frequent absence of oligoclonal bands favor NMO (Harrison p.3590).
Relying on oligoclonal bands, which are present in fewer than 20% of NMO patients (Harrison p.3590-3591).
Overlooking that NMO frequently coexists with systemic autoimmune disease, unlike MS (Harrison p.3591).

Failing to recognize AQP4-negative disease, where MOG antibodies may be present and where seronegative NMOSD requires both optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis to meet criteria (Harrison p.3591-3592).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading; diagnosis follows the 2015 International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria for NMOSD, which stratify by AQP4-IgG status. AQP4-IgG-positive disease requires at least one core clinical characteristic, a positive AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. AQP4-IgG-negative or unknown-status disease requires at least two core characteristics (one of which must be optic neuritis, acute myelitis with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, or area postrema syndrome), dissemination in space, fulfillment of additional MRI requirements, a negative or unavailable AQP4-IgG test, and exclusion of alternatives. Core clinical characteristics: optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem syndrome, symptomatic narcolepsy/acute diencephalic syndrome with typical MRI lesions, and symptomatic cerebral syndrome with typical brain lesions (Harrison p.3591, Table 456-1).
management: Treat acute attacks promptly with high-dose intravenous corticosteroids to limit attack-related injury
Use plasma exchange for severe or steroid-refractory attacks, which is critical because attacks drive permanent disability
Prevent relapses with long-term immunotherapy such as rituximab or an approved monoclonal agent targeting complement (eculizumab), the interleukin-6 receptor (satralizumab) or CD19 (inebilizumab)
Use oral immunosuppression with azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil under corticosteroid cover where biologics are unavailable
Avoid multiple sclerosis disease-modifying drugs such as interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod, which can worsen the disorder
Provide rehabilitation and symptomatic care for residual visual loss, spasticity, neuropathic pain and bladder dysfunction, with vigilance for respiratory compromise from cervical myelitis
Confirm the diagnosis with an AQP4-IgG cell-based assay and manage through a neuro-immunology service with long-term relapse monitoring
